slides.title: Total bilirubin
slides.eyebrow: Liver · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood; heel-stick blood in newborns

What it is used for: Used to check liver health, look for the cause of jaundice, find a bile duct blockage, monitor existing liver disease and check how well treatment works. It also helps diagnose disorders in which red blood cells break down too quickly, such as hemolytic anemia.

Commonly used to help diagnose newborn jaundice. Many healthy babies get it because their liver is not yet mature enough; it is usually harmless and clears within a few weeks, but in some cases high bilirubin can lead to brain damage, so infants are often tested as a precaution.

slides.title: Total bilirubin
slides.eyebrow: Liver · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Physiology: Bilirubin is a yellowish substance formed during the normal breakdown of old red blood cells and is found in bile. A healthy liver removes most of it through the bile ducts; if the liver is damaged or the ducts are blocked, bilirubin can leak into the blood, and too much can cause jaundice.

Jaundice arises in three ways: too many red cells break down (prehepatic, haemolytic); the liver is damaged or cannot process bilirubin (hepatic); bilirubin from the liver cannot reach the gut (posthepatic, obstructive — blocked bile ducts).

slides.title: Total bilirubin
cols: Possible causes of high bilirubin (hyperbilirubinemia): hemolytic anemia, liver disease and blockage of the bile ducts.
So a raised total bilirubin is fractionated.
Low bilirubin (hypobilirubinemia) is not usually a cause for concern; it may be due to medicines such as antibiotics, birth control pills, sleeping pills and seizure medicines.

slides.title: Total bilirubin
cols: Mainly indirect (unconjugated) — haemolysis or impaired conjugation such as Gilbert syndrome; direct (conjugated) — hepatocellular disease (e.g., viral or alcoholic hepatitis) or cholestasis/bile-duct obstruction.

slides.title: Total bilirubin
bullets: Pre-analytics: The provider may ask for fasting for several hours before the test. Tell the provider about all medicines taken; stop any only if the provider says so.
Interferences: An abnormal result does not always mean a condition that needs treatment: some medicines, certain foods and strenuous exercise can also raise bilirubin.

Limitations: Normal ranges vary between laboratories and with sex and age (infant or child). Bilirubin is only one measure of liver health; liver function tests, liver protein tests, urine tests, an ultrasound or a liver biopsy may also be needed.

slides.title: Total bilirubin
bullets: When liver test results are abnormal, the provider compares all the measured substances to look for patterns that suggest different types of liver conditions. Liver function tests alone usually cannot diagnose a specific disease.

Urine and stool help tell the types apart. Prehepatic: no bilirubin in urine (unconjugated bilirubin does not pass into urine), much urobilinogen, dark stool. Hepatic: bilirubin in urine, urobilinogen often raised. Posthepatic: bilirubin in urine (dark urine), little or no urobilinogen, pale clay-coloured stool. This is a general pattern — diagnosis relies on the clinical picture and other tests.

slides.title: Direct (conjugated) bilirubin
slides.eyebrow: Liver · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood
What it is used for: Direct (conjugated) bilirubin is one of the names under which bilirubin blood testing is done, alongside total and indirect (unconjugated) bilirubin.
Bilirubin blood testing is used to check liver health, look for the cause of jaundice, find out whether the bile ducts are blocked and monitor existing liver disease.

slides.title: Direct (conjugated) bilirubin
slides.eyebrow: Liver · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Physiology: Bilirubin forms during the normal breakdown of old red blood cells and is found in bile. A healthy liver removes most of it through the bile ducts; if the liver is damaged or the bile ducts are blocked, bilirubin can leak into the blood.

slides.title: Direct (conjugated) bilirubin
bullets: High: Most bilirubin circulates unconjugated. A raised conjugated (direct) bilirubin in most settings implies hepatocellular disease or biliary obstruction/cholestasis; this fraction is water-soluble and passes into urine, so bilirubin appears in urine.

slides.title: Direct (conjugated) bilirubin
bullets: Pre-analytics: The provider may ask for fasting for several hours before the test. Tell the provider about all medicines taken; stop any only if the provider says so.

Limitations: Bilirubin results are only one measure of liver health, and normal values vary by laboratory, sex and age (infant or child). Other tests, such as liver function tests, urine tests or an ultrasound, may be needed.

The MedlinePlus encyclopedia gives less than 0.3 mg/dL (5.1 µmol/L) as an example normal for direct bilirubin, but the reference depends on the laboratory and method — use the range on the report. Healthy urine normally contains no bilirubin.

slides.title: Jaundice and cholestasis
bullets: Bilirubin leaks into the blood when the liver is damaged or the bile ducts are blocked, causing jaundice. Liver tests are compared with each other to find patterns that suggest a type of liver condition; on their own they usually cannot diagnose a specific disease.

slides.title: Jaundice and cholestasis
rows: To look for the cause of jaundice, find a bile duct blockage and monitor liver disease.
High ALP from the liver may point to blocked bile ducts, cirrhosis or hepatitis.
Helps tell where ALP comes from: both rise in liver and bile duct disease, only ALP in bone disease.

slides.title: Jaundice and cholestasis
rows: Part of the liver panel; the pattern of results points to the type of liver condition.

slides.title: Jaundice and cholestasis
rows: A liver or bile duct disorder is likely (not bone).
A bone disorder is more likely.
Possible causes: hemolytic anemia, liver disease or blocked bile ducts — other tests tell them apart.
Prehepatic (haemolytic): indirect bilirubin ↑, no urine bilirubin, urobilinogen ↑, dark stool
Haemolysis or impaired conjugation such as Gilbert syndrome; check haemolysis markers.

slides.title: Jaundice and cholestasis
rows: Hepatic: both fractions ↑, urine bilirubin present, urobilinogen often ↑, ALT/AST predominate
Hepatocellular injury (e.g., viral or alcoholic hepatitis, cirrhosis).
Posthepatic (obstructive): direct bilirubin ↑, urine bilirubin present, urobilinogen ↓ or absent, pale stool; ALP and GGT predominate
Bile-duct obstruction (stone, tumour, stricture) likely — imaging is needed.
ALT/AST raised out of proportion to ALP (cytolysis)

slides.title: Jaundice and cholestasis
rows: Typical of alcoholic liver disease; in non-alcoholic disease a ratio above 1 may suggest cirrhosis.
Reduced liver synthetic function (hepatocellular failure) likely.

slides.title: Jaundice and cholestasis
bullets: Bilirubin is only one measure of liver health: liver function tests, urine tests, ultrasound or a liver biopsy may also be needed. Abnormal liver tests do not always mean liver disease.

slides.title: Prehepatic (haemolytic)
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Telling jaundice types apart
bullets: Blood bilirubin: Indirect (unconjugated) ↑
Urine bilirubin: Absent — this fraction does not enter urine
Urine urobilinogen: ↑
Stool: Dark
Causes: Haemolysis; impaired conjugation (Gilbert syndrome)

slides.title: Hepatic
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Telling jaundice types apart
bullets: Blood bilirubin: Both fractions ↑, including direct (conjugated)
Urine bilirubin: Present
Urine urobilinogen: Often ↑
Markers: ALT/AST predominate (cytolysis)
Causes: Viral or alcoholic hepatitis, cirrhosis, medicines

slides.title: Posthepatic (obstructive)
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Telling jaundice types apart
bullets: Blood bilirubin: Direct (conjugated) ↑
Urine bilirubin: Present (dark urine)
Urine urobilinogen: ↓ or absent
Stool: Pale, clay-coloured
Markers: ALP and GGT predominate (cholestasis)
Causes: Bile-duct stone, tumour, stricture

slides.title: Note
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Telling jaundice types apart
bullets: Jaundice arises in three ways: excess red-cell breakdown, liver damage, or bilirubin failing to reach the gut. This is a general scheme; diagnosis uses the clinical picture, imaging and other tests.

slides.title: Reference values and decision limits
slides.footnote: The reference interval varies by laboratory, method and population; the laboratory verifies its own interval (verification).

slides.title: Why are newborns often tested for bilirubin?
options: Newborn jaundice always means liver cancer
Many healthy newborns get jaundice because their liver is immature; it is usually harmless, but high bilirubin can sometimes damage the brain
Newborns cannot produce bilirubin, so any amount is abnormal
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: this is why infants are often tested as a precaution.

Basis: MedlinePlus: many healthy babies get jaundice because their livers haven't developed enough; in some cases high bilirubin can lead to brain damage, so infants are often tested as a precaution.

slides.title: Does a high bilirubin result on its own establish liver disease?
options: Yes — a high bilirubin always means liver disease, so other causes and further tests need not be considered
Yes, if the patient is also jaundiced, because jaundice proves the liver is the cause
No — it is only one measure of liver health, and medicines, foods or strenuous exercise can also raise it
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: further tests such as liver function tests, urine tests, ultrasound or biopsy may be needed.

Basis: MedlinePlus: a bilirubin blood test is only one measure of liver health; some medicines, certain foods or strenuous exercise can also raise bilirubin.

slides.title: Which statement about normal bilirubin values is correct?
options: They are the same in every laboratory, so any laboratory range can be applied
They depend only on sex and are the same for newborns and adults
They vary by laboratory, sex and whether the patient is an infant or child
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: this is why a result is compared with the reporting laboratory's own reference range.

Basis: MedlinePlus: normal results can vary based on the lab, sex and whether the test is done on an infant or child.

slides.title: According to the source, what happens to bilirubin when the bile ducts are blocked?
options: It can leak out of the liver into the blood
It is removed from the body faster than normal
The body stops producing bilirubin altogether
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: a healthy liver removes bilirubin through the bile ducts; when they are blocked, it leaks into the blood.

Basis: MedlinePlus: a healthy liver removes most bilirubin through the bile ducts; if the liver is damaged or the bile ducts are blocked, bilirubin can leak into the blood.

slides.title: Jaundice, bilirubin in urine, no urobilinogen, pale stool. Which type is most likely?
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct.

Basis: Without bile reaching the gut no urobilinogen forms and stool is pale; conjugated bilirubin enters urine — posthepatic (obstructive).

slides.title: Signs of cytolysis:
options: increased thymol turbidity test and decreased sublimate test

slides.title: Which test is important to examine for early diagnosis of acute viral hepatitis:
In the icteric form of acute viral hepatitis, the following is detected:
In which condition is an increase of free (unconjugated) bilirubin observed:
options: In Crigler-Najjar syndrome, in hemolysis of erythrocytes

slides.title: The most pronounced toxic effect of bilirubin occurs on:
The main part of conjugated bilirubin passes into:
Pigment metabolism. Bilirubin formation?
bullets: 1. 70–90% of bilirubin comes from the hemoglobin of aged erythrocytes: in macrophages heme oxygenase converts heme to biliverdin, and biliverdin reductase converts it to indirect (unconjugated) bilirubin; the rest comes from myoglobin, cytochromes and ineffective erythropoiesis.

2. Indirect bilirubin is insoluble in water and is transported in the blood bound to albumin to the liver; in the hepatocyte, with the participation of UGT1A1, it is conjugated with glucuronic acid (direct bilirubin) and excreted into the bile.

slides.title: Pigment metabolism. Bilirubin formation?
bullets: 3. In the intestine bacteria convert it to urobilinogen; part is reabsorbed (urobilinogen in urine), the rest is converted to stercobilin and colors the stool.

4. Disorders: hemolysis – indirect bilirubin rises; conjugation defects (Gilbert, Crigler-Najjar); hepatocellular injury – both fractions; cholestasis/obstruction – direct bilirubin, bilirubin in urine, stool becomes pale.
5. Laboratory: total and direct bilirubin (diazo reaction), indirect = total − direct; bilirubin and urobilinogen in urine; ALT/AST, ALP/GGT, hemolysis markers.

slides.title: Methods of determining bilirubin?
bullets: 1. The basic principle is the diazo reaction: bilirubin forms azobilirubin (colored) with diazotized sulfanilic acid; direct (conjugated) bilirubin reacts without an accelerator (caffeine-benzoate, etc.), total bilirubin with an accelerator (Jendrassik–Grof and its modifications).
2. Other methods: enzymatic/oxidative methods with vanadate or bilirubin oxidase; in newborns direct spectrophotometry (bilirubinometry) and transcutaneous measurement.
3. Indirect bilirubin is calculated: total − direct.
4. Preanalytics: bilirubin breaks down in light – keep the sample in the dark; interference from hemolysis and lipemia.

slides.title: Methods of determining bilirubin?
bullets: 5. The reference interval depends on the laboratory, unit µmol/L (for example StatPearls: total bilirubin 2–17, direct 0–6 µmol/L; normally <1 mg/dL ≈ 17 µmol/L); interpret the result together with liver enzymes and hemolysis markers.

slides.title: Pigment metabolism. Methods of determining bilirubin in blood serum?
bullets: 1. Pigment metabolism: heme → biliverdin → indirect bilirubin (with albumin) → conjugation by UGT1A1 in the liver → direct bilirubin into bile → in the intestine urobilinogen/stercobilin.
2. Determination in serum – diazo reaction: direct bilirubin without an accelerator, total bilirubin with an accelerator (Jendrassik–Grof-type methods); indirect = total − direct.
3. Alternative methods: vanadate/enzymatic oxidation; in newborns direct spectrophotometry.
4. Preanalytics: protect from light, avoid hemolysis.

slides.title: Pigment metabolism. Methods of determining bilirubin in blood serum?
bullets: 5. Interpretation: predominance of indirect – hemolysis or conjugation disorder; predominance of direct – cholestasis or hepatocellular injury; result in µmol/L.
